title: Building trust and resilience through secure software practices
snippet: Learn how Sage uses the Software Security Code of Practice to strengthen assurance, collaboration, and continuous improvement in the wider digital ecosystem. The post Building trust and resilience through secure software practices appeared first on Sage Advice UK.
fullText:
Key takeaways

Sage used the UK Government’s Software Security Code of Practice to assess its established security, governance, and assurance practices across the Copilot Factory Framework (CFF).

The assessment reinforced our existing approach of embedding security throughout the software lifecycle to strengthen the resilience of AI-powered services.

The assessment validated established security practices, including access reviews, third-party dependency controls, vulnerability management, and security documentation, while helping Sage make the supporting governance and evidence more explicit.

Cross-functional collaboration between Security, Product engineering, Architecture, and Cloud Operations provided a more complete view of how security controls are understood and applied across the software lifecycle.

Organisations can use the Software Security Code of Practice as a practical framework for continuous improvement, stronger customer assurance, and greater cyber resilience.

Digital services are central to how businesses manage finances, people, and operations. As reliance on software grows, and AI capabilities become embedded across more products, users need confidence that security is built into how the technology is designed, developed, and maintained.

At Sage, security is built into how we design, develop and evolve our software, with our approach continually advancing as our products, technology and the threat landscape change.

As signatories of the UK Government’s Cyber Resilience Pledge and ambassadors of the Software Security Code of Practice, we’re committed to finding practical ways to test our security approach, learn from the process, and help promote stronger security across the wider software ecosystem, while encouraging our partners to do the same.

Here’s what we talk about in this article:

Why Sage supports the Cyber Resilience Pledge 

Cyber resilience is not only a technical priority. It is essential to business continuity, customer confidence, and responsible innovation. By supporting the Pledge and the Code, Sage is reinforcing its commitment to secure software practices and collaboration between government and industry. This collaboration helps translate shared security principles into practical action: government provides a clear and consistent framework, while industry applies it in real operating environments and shares practical insights to support its continued relevance and wider adoption.

Our involvement with the Code reflects our broader responsibility to contribute beyond our own organisation. By sharing practical experience, Sage can help other organisations understand how the Code can be applied, encourage partners to adopt stronger practices and provide constructive industry insight into how voluntary frameworks work in practice. This helps build a more consistent approach to software security across the wider ecosystem and keep the focus on sustained resilience rather than one-off compliance. 

The approach

Sage selected the Copilot Factory Framework (CFF) for assessment against the Software Security Code of Practice as it provides AI capabilities that can be used across multiple products. This made it a meaningful test of whether established security practices could be demonstrated consistently in a shared, fast-evolving technology environment.

The CFF provides a scalable foundation for delivering AI-powered experiences across Sage products, enabling teams to build and deploy AI capabilities using consistent governance, security controls, and approved technologies. Assessing a shared platform therefore offered value beyond a single service: it tested the foundations that product teams rely on when bringing AI capabilities to customers.

The assessment was not simply about confirming alignment with individual controls. It examined how security decisions, evidence, and responsibilities connect across the full lifecycle and whether that approach could provide clear assurance to the teams that depend on the CFF.

The assessment brought together colleagues from Security, Product, Engineering, Architecture and Cloud Operations.

A dedicated security lead coordinated the collection and validation of evidence, and an independent third party, NCC Group, reviewed the evidence against the Code’s controls.

The independent review confirmed established strengths and created a clear route for further improvement. In particular, it showed where greater clarity, formality, and consistency would make existing governance easier to apply, evidence, and understand across teams.

Key outcomes and lessons learned

Embedding security throughout design and development 

The review reinforced the importance of building security into design and development decisions for the CFF. This includes the consistent governance of third-party services, software components, dependencies, and licences from the outset, supported by clear and accessible evidence. Embedding these practices early strengthens traceability, supports compliance, and helps product teams identify and address software security risks before delivery.

Validating assurance around the build environment 

The review validated the controls that protect the integrity and security of the software build environment, including managed access, strong authentication, infrastructure-as-code, and audit logging. It also identified an opportunity to introduce greater formality and consistency through repeatable access reviews, providing ongoing assurance that access remains appropriate and aligned with business need.

Validating secure deployment and maintenance

The review considered how vulnerabilities are identified, prioritised, and managed throughout the software lifecycle. It validated the effectiveness of existing vulnerability management practices against the Software Security Code of Practice, including automated security scanning, penetration testing, and defined remediation targets. The outcome was stronger assurance that risks are addressed according to their significance and managed consistently throughout the lifecycle. For teams using the CFF, this provides greater confidence that vulnerabilities affecting a shared platform can be identified and acted on in a structured and timely way.

Clarifying service commitments

Because the CFF primarily provides AI services to other Sage products, some of the Code’s requirements needed to be considered in the context of internal product customers.

The review validated the service governance supporting the CFF, including established support and communication processes, lifecycle management, and commitments around service retirement. It also identified opportunities to express these practices with greater clarity and formality. This provides dependent teams with greater transparency and predictability, reduces operational risk, enables more effective planning, and supports reliable service delivery across the organisation.

Advice and insights for other organisations

For organisations considering using the Code, our experience highlighted four practical ways to gain greater value from the assessment:

Use the Code as a catalyst for improvement. The greatest value can come from the conversations the assessment creates and the opportunities it reveals. Clearly expressed governance and ownership can deliver greater clarity, accountability, and assurance. 

Formalise what already works. Strong practices may already exist, but clear ownership, documented commitments and accessible evidence make it easier to demonstrate that controls are operating as intended. 

Bring the right people together early. Software security spans across more than one function. Involving Security, Product, Engineering, Architecture, and Cloud Operations creates a complete view of how security is applied across the lifecycle. 

Share practical learning. Implementation experience can help other organisations apply the Code, support wider adoption, and strengthen resilience across the software ecosystem.

Final thoughts: Future commitments

The Software Security Code of Practice offers organisations a valuable opportunity to strengthen security, build customer trust, and demonstrate responsible leadership.

For organisations considering the Code, the first step is to assess how its principles align with existing practices, identify where ownership or evidence could be strengthened, and involve the right teams early. The wider opportunity is to use the assessment not only to improve internal assurance, but also to contribute practical insight that helps raise standards across the industry.

Sage continues to advocate for the Code beyond our own assessment by sharing practical expertise and encouraging participation across our partner ecosystem. 

This extends the value of government-industry collaboration: lessons learned from implementation can support wider adoption, strengthen collective resilience and demonstrate how common principles can be applied in different operating environments. 

Read on Zynk: one of our Sage partner case study and their adoption of the Department for Science, Innovation and Technology’s Software Security Code of Practice. Showing how and advocacy can help extend common security principles through the wider partner ecosystem.

title: Beyond the brief: Where do accountants’ hidden hours go?
snippet: Providing business-critical advice, reassurance and answering unexpected client questions all take time. Discover what The Hidden Hours of Accountancy conversation reveals about accountants’ changing workload, and how practices can make that work more visible. The post Beyond the brief: Where do accountants’ hidden hours go? appeared first on Sage Advice UK.
fullText:
Key takeaways

Accountants’ hidden hours include the advice, reassurance and coordination surrounding their core services.

The Hidden Hours of Accountancy research from Sage found that 81% of accountants work outside their scope, highlighting how widely support extends beyond the agreed brief.

Accountants can discuss current figures with clients without waiting for records to arrive. But both sides need to agree who keeps those records up to date and when the accountant will review them.

Technology can save processing time while introducing demands around learning, client support and ongoing oversight.

Recognising recurring extra work helps practices plan their services, improve workflows and set clearer expectations.

Ask an accountant what they’d do with five extra hours a week, and the answer can be surprisingly personal.

“I’d probably stop working on a Saturday,” said Andrew Dick, owner of G W Dick & Co.

His answer points to a pattern many accountants and bookkeepers will recognise, and it’s what we discuss in this article, as follows:

Alongside the agreed work sits another layer: the client question that turns into a conversation about the future of the business, the reassurance before a big decision, the software problem that lands in your inbox. 

The Hidden Hours of Accountancy research from Sage found that 81% of respondents work outside their scope.

In the first The Hidden Hours of Accountancy episode, which you can watch above, Andrew and Julie Young, managing directors of Walter Dawson & Son Accountants, explore where that time goes. They go on to explain why the support that makes a client relationship valuable can also make the workload harder to contain.

Accountants’ hidden hours are the time spent on work surrounding their core services, some of which goes unbilled. That can include chasing information, explaining requirements, answering unexpected questions, helping clients navigate software and providing reassurance when a business decision feels difficult.

Some of this work is necessary to complete an agreed task. Some develops as clients bring more of their concerns to someone they trust. During a busy day, there may be little opportunity to consider how each request fits into the service being paid for.

In the video above, Andrew describes how closely business and personal concerns overlap for small business owners. A problem in the business affects life at home, while a family issue can influence what happens at work. An accountant may become the first person a client approaches because they already understand the business and its history.

Julie describes a similar instinct to help. Asking more questions and understanding what a client wants to achieve can reveal what they actually need from their accountant.

These conversations have professional value. They can lead to better advice and a clearer understanding of the client’s goals. The difficulty is accounting for the time they take and the responsibility they create. When the work stays hidden, it becomes easy to underestimate the time and capacity it really takes to serve its clients well.

How client support grows beyond the brief

Additional support often grows through ordinary interactions. A client asks a question, their accountant helps, and the client gains confidence in them.

Over time, this can become a continuous relationship. Clients want to discuss decisions while they still have options, and accountants have an opportunity to help before a commitment has been made.

Julie’s discussion of ongoing client relationships shows why this matters. Understanding what a client is considering gives an accountant more room to offer useful advice than discovering the decision later in the records.

But the same willingness to help can make it difficult to recognise when the service has expanded. Julie acknowledges that accountants can give valuable support away because they care about their clients and want to solve the problem in front of them.

The Hidden Hours of Accountancy research found that 70% of accountants said their fees do not reflect the support they provide. Alongside Julie’s experience, that finding raises a question about how clearly the full service is understood and recognised.

The client experiences a helpful answer. The accountant fits another conversation between existing commitments. Neither necessarily pauses to discuss whether this is an occasional request or the start of an ongoing need.

Across a client base, those decisions add up. What looks like a manageable favour in isolation can become a regular part of the working week.

The same pattern showed up at Accountex Summit Manchester. Ask the Accountant podcast host Aaron Patrick described how the first Making Tax Digital (MTD) for Income Tax quarterly update exposed work his practice had underestimated.

Having participated in the beta programme since 2022, he was confident about filing. Getting clients signed up, receiving their data on time and helping them understand the change proved more challenging.

“I had to completely and utterly rip up my capacity planning,” he said.

For the next stage, his practice was bringing engagement letters forward and setting clearer expectations about fees and what clients needed to provide. Aaron also recognised that repeated communication from his practice did not mean every client understood the change: some were still hearing about it for the first time.

His experience shows why the conversations around a service need space in the plan. Explaining the change, agreeing responsibilities and getting clients ready all take time before the submission itself.

Making that surrounding work visible gives both sides a better basis for discussing the service. Clients can understand what is involved, while practices can plan for the support surrounding the task as well as the task itself.

Why technology changes where the time goes

Technology can make information available sooner and reduce the effort required for individual tasks. It also changes what accountants need to understand and what clients may expect them to do.

Julie describes earlier access to client records as an important change in the profession. When information is available throughout the year, accountants can use it to support decisions closer to the moment they are being made.

That creates opportunities for more timely conversations. Instead of waiting for a client to bring in records, an accountant can work with information already available in the software.

In episode one of The Hidden Hours of Accountancy video series, Andrew highlights the learning involved. Accountants may need to understand several platforms, keep up with changes and help clients work through unfamiliar processes.

A practice can therefore become faster at processing information while spending more time on the activities around it. Looking only at the time technology saves on one task can miss where the work has moved across the rest of the working week.

Continuous access also raises questions about responsibility. Andrew points out that boundaries can become less clear when an accountant can see into a client’s software throughout the year.

A client may assume that someone is watching for problems. Their accountant may expect to review the records at agreed points. Both can believe the other is taking care of something unless the arrangement is made explicit.

Who maintains the records? Who checks them, and how often? What should prompt the client to get in touch?

Answering those questions helps turn shared access into a workable service. It also makes the limits of that service easier to understand.

A useful starting point is to look at what happens during a normal working week.

Which questions recur? Where do you repeatedly chase information? What software problems do clients bring to you? Which conversations regularly grow beyond the original request?

Recording those patterns can help a practice see where its capacity goes. It can also distinguish valuable support that deserves a clearer place in the service from avoidable administration.

1. Recognise recurring support

If the same kind of request keeps appearing, it may reflect an ongoing client need.

A regular planning conversation, clearer guidance or a defined support arrangement could serve the client better than a series of urgent requests. Recognising the pattern gives you something specific to discuss.

The aim is to understand how the relationship has developed and whether the service still fits.

2. Agree who does what

Where records and software are shared, explain responsibilities in practical terms.

Clients need to know what information they should maintain, what you will review and when they should raise a concern. Clear expectations can reduce uncertainty and give both sides more confidence in the arrangement.

These conversations are particularly useful when introducing software or changing a working process, because familiar assumptions may no longer apply.

3. Review the steps around the task

Look at the process as well as the final activity. Repeated requests for information, disconnected systems and unclear handovers can all add effort.

Aaron described how his practice was using embedded accounting with clients working in Tide.

His clients categorised payments in their banking app, with those categories coming through to his accounting system for review. This allowed them to contribute information through a tool they already used, while the practice retained the work of checking and correcting it.

For Aaron, the appeal was reducing friction in the client relationship. His example also provides a useful way to assess a connected workflow: does it make information easier to provide and review, and is it clear where the accountant’s attention and judgement are still needed?

4. Make room for judgement

Some conversations need time. Understanding a business owner’s ambitions or helping them think through a difficult decision can be central to good advice.

Making this work visible helps a practice decide how to accommodate it. It creates a firmer basis for planning capacity and discussing the service when a client’s needs change.

What would five hours back make possible?

Towards the end of the episode, the conversation turns to what getting five hours back would mean.

The question brings the discussion back to the people doing the work. Time saved has value because of what it makes possible, whether that is a more considered client conversation, space to work on the practice or an evening with fewer unfinished tasks on your mind.

The Hidden Hours of Accountancy research found that 77% of accountants struggle to switch off. That gives the discussion of capacity a personal consequence. How work is organised can affect what people carry beyond the end of the working day.

Julie would invest some of the time in thinking about her own business and how to move it forward. Helping clients can absorb so much attention that there is little space left to consider the practice’s own goals.

Their answers reveal two things hidden hours can displace: time away from work and time to plan its future. For Andrew, getting time back would mean a Saturday away from work. For Julie, it would mean space to plan the future of her own practice—the kind of thinking she helps clients do for theirs.

Final thoughts

Start with your own last working week. Identify one recurring piece of work that has grown beyond the agreed service. Is it support that needs a clearer place, an expectation that needs discussing or a process that could work better?

Use that example to begin a conversation with your team or client about what should change.

Getting time back starts with understanding where it is going. Making hidden work visible gives you the opportunity to decide what should be valued, redesigned or simply done differently.

Frequently asked questions

			

			

	

How can accountants spot scope creep early?

	

			

Look for repeated requests extending beyond the agreed service, such as ongoing software support, additional analysis or frequent advice on new decisions. Consider their cumulative effect on time and responsibility. A recurring pattern provides a basis for discussing the client’s changing needs.

	

	

Does access to client software mean an accountant is monitoring it continuously?

	

			

Access alone does not establish a review schedule. Clients and accountants should agree who maintains information, how often reviews happen and which issues the client needs to raise. Those expectations should be reflected clearly in the service arrangement.

	

	

How can accountants explain additional work to clients?

	

			

Describe the work in specific terms and connect it to the client’s needs. Explain how the requests relate to the existing service, then discuss an arrangement that supports them going forward. Using concrete examples makes the conversation easier to understand and plan around.
